metadata.title: Highway Networks (Srivastava, Greff, Schmidhuber, 2015)
metadata.framework: Gated shortcut connections allowing learned regulation of information flow in very deep networks
metadata.source_note: Extraction based on well-known content of arXiv:1505.00387.

nodes.name: Difficulty of training very deep networks
nodes.statement: Despite theoretical and empirical evidence that depth is crucial for neural network performance, training very deep networks (tens to hundreds of layers) with SGD is extremely difficult. Gradient-based optimization struggles because gradients either vanish or explode across many layers, and standard feedforward architectures provide no mechanism to ease information flow through the network.

nodes.name: Highway network layer formulation
nodes.statement: A highway network layer computes $\mathbf{y} = H(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{W}_H) \cdot T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{W}_T) + \mathbf{x} \cdot C(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{W}_C)$, where $H$ is a nonlinear transform (e.g., affine + ReLU), $T$ is the transform gate, and $C$ is the carry gate. Setting $C = 1 - T$ (a common simplification) gives $\mathbf{y} = H(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{W}_H) \cdot T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{W}_T) + \mathbf{x} \cdot (1 - T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{W}_T))$. The gate $T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{W}_T) = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_T \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_T)$ is a sigmoid function that learns to interpolate between the transform and carry (identity) behaviors.

nodes.name: Transform gate
nodes.statement: The transform gate $T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{W}_T) = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_T \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_T) \in [0,1]^d$ controls how much of the nonlinear transform $H(\mathbf{x})$ passes through. When $T \to 0$, the layer output is $\mathbf{x}$ (pure carry / identity); when $T \to 1$, the output is $H(\mathbf{x})$ (standard nonlinear layer). The gate bias $\mathbf{b}_T$ is typically initialized to negative values (e.g., $-1$ to $-3$) so the network starts close to identity and learns which layers need to transform.

nodes.name: Information highways
nodes.statement: Highway networks allow unimpeded information flow across many layers on 'information highways'. When the transform gate is close to zero for all layers, the input propagates through the network almost unchanged, analogous to how LSTM gates allow information to persist across many time steps in recurrent networks.

nodes.name: Relationship to LSTM gating
nodes.statement: The highway network architecture is inspired by LSTM recurrent networks. The transform gate $T$ is analogous to the LSTM input gate, and the carry gate $C = 1 - T$ is analogous to the LSTM forget gate. This transfers the LSTM's ability to learn long-range dependencies across time to the feedforward setting across depth.

nodes.name: Highway networks enable training of very deep networks
nodes.statement: Highway networks with hundreds of layers can be trained directly using stochastic gradient descent with a variety of activation functions. The gating mechanism allows gradient flow through the network even at extreme depths, avoiding the vanishing gradient problem that prevents training of plain deep feedforward networks.
assumptions: Highway layer with transform and carry gates (DP_HW.2)
conclusions: Successful optimization of networks with 50-900+ layers

nodes.name: MNIST with very deep highway networks
nodes.statement: Highway networks with up to 900 layers are trained on MNIST. All highway networks converge, while plain networks of 20+ layers fail to converge. Highway networks with 50-100 layers achieve the best results. The gate biases learn meaningful patterns: early and late layers tend to have gates closer to identity, while middle layers apply stronger transformations.

nodes.name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 results
nodes.statement: Highway networks with 20-100 layers on CIFAR-10/100 outperform plain networks of the same depth. A highway network with thin layers (using Fitnets-style architecture) achieves competitive results with significantly fewer parameters than wider shallow networks.

nodes.name: Highway network training with gate bias initialization
nodes.statement: Highway networks are trained with SGD. The key training detail is the initialization of the transform gate bias $\mathbf{b}_T$ to negative values (e.g., $-1, -2, -3$), which initializes the network close to the identity function. This allows the network to start by copying inputs through and gradually learn which layers should transform. No special training schedule or auxiliary losses are needed.
